E:\\videos\\mickey5\\wt\\vlog\\mickey5\\.text: Your turkey comes out dry because of one thing nobody ever told you. The white meat is done 20 degrees before the dark meat. So by the time the legs are ready, the breast is already sawdust. Tonight I'll show you the old Boston butcher trick that fixes it, and it costs you one bag of ice. Never roast your turkey dry again, my friend. Last Thanksgiving, a nice lady came back to my counter the Monday after. $74 that's what she paid for a 16 pound fresh turkey at one of those fancy markets she roasted it 4 and a half hours until the little red button popped out of the breast just like the bag said she said Mickey the skin was beautiful and the breast was like eating a paper towel her son-in-law poured gravy on it like he was putting out a fire and here's the part that hurts she did everything they told her She waited for that little button.

And that button was the problem. It doesn't pop until the breast is way past done. Nobody ever told her that. So here's my promise. By the end of this video, you'll put a turkey on the table with juicy white meat and dark meat that falls off the bone, both done at the same time. Eight old tricks from 54 years behind this counter. The folks who sell those little pop-up buttons won't love me for this one And trick number four, the ice on the breast is the one my customers call me about every December For the new folks, I'm Mickey, Mickey Callahan I run a narrow little butcher shop in Dorchester, Boston and I've been behind this counter since 1972 My father had the shop before me Every November, this place is wall-to-wall turkeys, names on tags, folks lined up out the door into the cold. Last time I told you how to pick and cook a holiday ham.

Today it's the big bird because I've heard every dry turkey story there is and they all come down to the same few mistakes. Trick number one starts at the store. Turn the turkey over and read the label. If it says basted or self-basting or contains up to 8% solution, that bird's been pumped full of salt water and flavoring. you're paying turkey prices for that water and it cooks up soft and spongy and it's too salty to brine buy a plain turkey fresh or frozen nothing added and don't buy too big figure about a pound and a half per person that covers dinner and sandwiches a 12 to 14 pound bird is the sweet spot past 18 pounds the outside dries out before the middle gets there If you've got a big crowd, roast two small birds, not one giant. Fresh or frozen, that's up to you.

A good frozen turkey was frozen hard the day it was packed, and it's every bit as good if you thaw it right. A fresh one should feel cold and firm, not soft, with no smell and no puddle of pink water in the bag. And look at the skin. You want it creamy white and dry, not gray, not torn, not slimy. Trick number two, thaw it right and start sooner than you think. In the refrigerator, give it one day for every four to five pounds. That 14-pound turkey needs three full days. Put it in on Sunday for a Thursday dinner in a pan on the bottom shelf so it doesn't drip on anything. Never on the counter and never in hot water. The outside sits warm for hours while the middle is still ice. If you're late, put it in the sink in cold water, still in its wrapper, and change the water every 30 minutes, about 30 minutes a pound. But the refrigerator is always better.

How do you know it's thawed? Reach inside the cavity. If you feel ice, it's not ready. Pull out the bag of giblets in the neck. Don't forget them. Everybody's grandmother roasted that paper bag at least once. The neck goes in a pot with an onion and water, and that's the start of your gravy. trick number three is the dry brine forget the big bucket of salt water it's messy it takes up the whole refrigerator and it gives you wet rubbery skin here's what we do kosher salt about one tablespoon for every four or five pounds of turkey that 14 pound bird three tablespoons pat the turkey dry then slide your fingers under the skin of the breast and the thighs gently and rub about half the salt right on the meat. The rest goes all over the outside. Then put it on a rack in a pan uncovered in the refrigerator for one to three days.

The salt goes in, pulls the juice in with it, and the meat holds on to that juice in the oven. And the cold air dries the skin out like paper. That's how you get skin that crackles. Don't rinse it. Just pat it dry and go. Trick number four. This is the old Boston trick, and it's the one that fixes the problem from the start of this video. Ice on the breast. The breast is done at about 160. the thighs want 175. So you want the breast to start colder than the legs. An hour before it goes in the oven, take the turkey out of the refrigerator and set it on the counter. Fill two zipper bags with ice and lay them right on top of the breast. Cover the bags with a towel. The legs sit out and warm up. The breast stays ice cold. When it goes in the oven, the breast is starting maybe 10 or 15 degrees colder than the thighs.

So it takes longer to get done, and the whole bird finishes together. My father learned that from an old German butcher on Blue Hill Avenue in 1950-something. One bag of ice. That's the whole trick. Now people ask me, Mickey, isn't that dangerous, leaving a turkey out for an hour? An hour is fine. The bird is still cold to the bone, and the oven is about to take care of everything on the surface. What you never do is leave it out all afternoon. One hour, ice on the breast, then straight into a hot oven and take the ice bags off first. I've had two customers forget. Trick number five is how you set up the oven. Rack in the lower third, turkey on a rack in a heavy roasting pan, breast up, wings tucked under and put the legs toward the back of the oven the back is the hottest part and the legs are the part that needs the heat start hot

425 degrees for the first 30 minutes to get that skin going. Then turn it down to 325 for the rest. A 14-pound bird usually takes about three hours all in. But you don't go by the clock. You go by the thermometer. And don't stuff the bird. The stuffing in the middle has to get to 165 to be safe. And by then your breast is dry as a bone. Bake the stuffing in a dish on the side. Put an onion, a lemon, and a few sprigs of thyme inside the turkey instead. Rub the skin all over with a couple tablespoons of soft butter or oil and a little pepper. No more salt. The brine already did that. And then shut the door and leave it alone. Don't baste it every half hour. Every time you open that door, the oven drops 50 degrees and basting only wets the skin you just dried for three days. trick number six

Throw away that little pop-up button. It's set to pop way too hot, and that's how that lady lost her breast meat. Buy a real thermometer. It costs less than the gravy. Check the breast in the thickest part, near the bone but not touching it. When it reads 160, check the thigh, deep in, next to the body. You want 175 in the thigh. When both are there, it comes out. Start checking a good 45 minutes before you think it's ready. Here's a little test for the doubters. Poke the thigh with a fork. The juice that runs out should be clear, not pink. And wiggle the drumstick. if it moves loose in the joint like an old door hinge the dark meets ready but the thermometer is the only thing that never lies so trust the numbers first and if the breast is getting there first anyway lay a piece of foil just over the breast like a little shield

The legs keep going, the breast slows down. Trick number seven, let it rest. 30 to 40 minutes on the board before anybody touches it. A big bird stays hot a long time, and the breast climbs another 5 degrees while it sits, right up to 165. That's done and safe, and still juicy. Don't wrap it tight in foil. that steams the skin you worked three days for. Just a loose sheet over the top and use that time. That's when you make the gravy from the drippings in the pan. Here's how my mother made the gravy. Pour the drippings into a measuring cup and let the fat rise. Spoon three tablespoons of that fat back into the pan. Whisk in three tablespoons of flour and cook it two minutes till it smells like toast. Then whisk in the drippings and the next stock, about three cups, and let it bubble till it coats a spoon. Salt and pepper last.

Trick number eight is how you carve it, and this is the butcher's way. Don't stand at the table sawing thin slices off the side of the bird. Take the legs off first at the joint. Then run your knife down along the breastbone and take each breast off in one whole piece. Lay the whole breast flat on the board and slice it across against the grain, about half an inch thick. Every slice gets a little skin on top It stays juicier It looks beautiful on the platter And you're done in 5 minutes Then the carcass goes in the pot for soup And don't forget the dark meat Pull the thigh off the drumstick at the joint Then slice the thigh meat off the bone Put the drumsticks on the platter hoe For the folks who like to hold one The dark meat is the most forgiving part of the whole bird and with the ice trick it'll be falling off the bone. Skin still pale and the meat's almost done? Turn the oven up to 450 for the last 10 minutes and watch it. Breast done and the thighs aren't? Take the breast off the bone, cover it, and put the legs back in for 20 minutes. Nobody will ever know. Still frozen Thursday morning? Cold water in the sink? Every Thanksgiving morning, he'd come in at five, the shop still dark, and he'd hand out the last turkeys to the folks who forgot to order. Then he'd go home and roast ours with two bags of ice on the breast, and my mother would laugh at him every single year. She stopped laughing when she tasted it. Sixty years later, I still do it exactly the same way, and my grandson thinks I invented it. Now the arithmetic. That lady paid $74 for 16 pounds and the whole breast went in the trash.
